chunks: What a regular expression is. The question: What is regex?
A regular expression, or regex, is a short pattern that describes a whole set of text strings.
Instead of searching for one exact word, you describe a shape, such as "VDD= then a number then V". A regex engine then finds, pulls out or replaces whatever fits.
Hardware engineers use regexes to dig voltages, addresses and error codes out of long logs and reports.
Think of a license plate rule: three letters, then four digits. That rule describes millions of plates without listing any. A regex is that kind of rule for text.
It has fixed parts, like the letters VDD, and flexible parts, like "any run of digits". It can describe a shape.
It cannot count unlimited nesting, such as matching every opening bracket with its closing one. For that you need a real parser (a program built to read nested structure).
The state machine for the regex ab c . S0 waits for a ; S1 loops on each b (that is the ); c moves to the accepting state S2.
Any other input has no transition, which means no match.
A hardware pattern-matcher (for example in network packet inspection) implements exactly such machines with a state register and next-state logic ("What is an FSM?")
Character class: a set of allowed characters in square brackets. [0-9 amps-Fa-f] is one hex digit (0 to 9 or A to F, the digits of base 16).
Quantifier: how many times the item before it may repeat. + means one or more, and means zero or more.
Capture group: parentheses that mark the part of a match you want to pull out. Greedy vs lazy: a greedy quantifier takes as much text as it can, and a lazy one takes as little.
Anchor: a marker for a position rather than a character, such as ^ for the start of a line.
A log line reads VDD=3. 29 volts IDD=12. 5 milliamps addr=0x1F4 amps . In the pattern VDD=(\d+\. \d+)V , \d+ means one or more digits, \.
means a literal dot, and the parentheses capture the number. It returns 3. 29 . The pattern 0x[0-9 amps-Fa-f]+ finds the hex address 0x1F4 amps . One trap is greediness.
On <b x</b <b y</b , <b . </b matches the whole string, but the lazy <b . ? </b matches only <b x</b . That is the whole idea.
"A regex is a compact pattern language for describing sets of strings so you can search, extract or replace text.
Building blocks are literals, character classes, quantifiers like and + , anchors, groups and alternation. I use them to parse logs and reports, like pulling VDD=3.
29 volts out of a test log with VDD=(\d+\. \d+)V . Watch out for greedy versus lazy matching and catastrophic backtracking.
Theoretically they correspond to finite state machines, so they can't handle nested structures."
